eBay Buyer Protection in the UK: What You Need to Know to Stay Safe

eBay offers buyer protection in the UK, but knowing how to use it properly is essential to stay safe from online marketplace fraud.

By Beat the Scam Editorial Team · Published 2026-04-17 · 1 min read

eBay buyer protectioneBay scams UKmarketplace fraudnon-delivery claimsitem not as describedonline shopping safetydelivery scam UKparcel scamfake delivery textonline marketplace scam UKbuying and selling scam UK
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.
On this page
  1. Quick answer
  2. Warning signs
  3. How this scam usually works
  4. How to verify safely

Quick answer

This guide explains eBay's buyer protection programme for UK customers, including how to file claims for non-delivery and item not as described cases. Discover red flags to watch for, best practices when purchasing, and what to do if you fall victim to a scam on the platform.

Warning signs

  • Pressure to act immediately
  • Requests for payment, login details, or one-time codes
  • Suspicious links or domains
  • Requests for upfront payment
  • Messages that create urgency or fear

How this scam usually works

Scammers impersonate trusted names such as eBay to extract money, account access, or personal information. The usual pattern is urgency, impersonation, and a push to click a link or send payment.

How to verify safely

Go to the official website manually, verify the domain carefully, and use independently verified contact details before taking any action.

What to do if you already interacted

Change passwords immediately, contact your bank if payment details were involved, keep evidence, and report the incident through the relevant UK channel such as Action Fraud.

Frequently asked questions

Is eBay a scam?

eBay itself may be legitimate, but scammers often impersonate it. Always verify the source independently before acting.

How can I verify eBay safely?

Use the official website directly, avoid message links, and confirm contact details through trusted public sources.

What should I do if I already interacted?

Change passwords, contact your bank if needed, keep evidence, and report the incident through the relevant UK reporting route.

Fast checks

  • Pause before sending money or credentials
  • Verify with an official site, app, or number
  • Never share one-time passcodes
  • Be sceptical of bank transfer pressure
